title: LSH-driven prefix clustering, GPU prewarm profiles, and cross-request dedupe
creator: Riley Chen
description:
Goal: Reduce redundant KV storage and GPU warmup overhead by grouping semantically similar prefixes into clusters (approximate matching) using locality-sensitive hashing (LSH), then maintaining lightweight GPU prewarm profiles for each cluster to accelerate KV residency and increase cross-request cache reuse.

Problem statement: Exact prefix fingerprinting does not capture small variations in user prompts (templated substitutions, punctuation, minor reordering), which leads to missed reuse opportunities and unnecessary KV duplication. Warmup costs to bring slabs/fragments into GPU memory for cold clusters are high and add tail latency for first requests. Continuous batching can improve throughput but still wastes GPU memory when similar but not identical prefixes are treated as distinct.

Scope: Implement an LSH-based prefix similarity index at the request router level, a cluster-to-KV manifest mapping, and an LRU+frequency prewarm profile per cluster. Integrate cluster signals into the continuous batching scheduler so that requests from warm clusters are prioritized to hit GPU-resident KV slices, and speculative prefetching can bring high-probability cluster fragments into memory during load spikes.

Key deliverables:
- LSH index service (ApproxMatch) that produces stable cluster IDs for incoming prefixes (configurable hash families and similarity thresholds).
- Cluster manifest store mapping cluster IDs -> list of canonical fragment IDs and resident GPU slab references.
- GPU prewarm profile controller that tracks per-cluster heat and issues async prefetches when heat exceeds threshold. Profiles are compact (Bloom filters or compact bitmaps) to avoid memory blowup.
- Changes to batching scheduler: affinity buckets for cluster IDs so batches preferentially coalesce requests from same cluster where latency SLOs allow.
- Metrics, dashboards, and smoke tests to validate reduced duplication and warmup latency improvements.
comments: 2026-02-12 - Kickoff: Reviewed trade-offs with Research (Ethan Morris) and Runtime (Sofia Kim). Decision: use L2-normalized token embedding vectors (first-pass fast model) + LSH over token embeddings to keep runtime cheap. Prototype to profile cost of LSH step under 10k req/s.

2026-02-20 - Prototype: implemented a Go-based LSH service using signed random projections. End-to-end prototype shows 18% additional cache hits on sampled traffic when threshold tuned to 0.82 cosine sim. Memory overhead for LSH tables ~6MB per shard. Saved ~12% GPU warmup tokens in synthetic replay.

2026-02-25 - Design review feedback from PM (Evan Li): prefer conservative thresholds for multi-tenant environments to avoid cross-tenant contamination. Action: add tenant-scoped namespaces to cluster IDs and enforce tenant isolation for manifest resolution.

2026-03-02 - Eng review (runtime): identified race in prewarm controller where concurrent eviction could remove fragments mid-prefetch. Plan: add prewarm reservations and avoid eviction for N seconds after prefetch completes. Also add metrics for prewarm failures.

2026-03-08 - Security review request filed: ensure LSH cluster IDs are deterministic but non-reversible to avoid prompt leakage. We will salt tenant IDs and rotate salts quarterly. Security: Alyssa Park engaged.

2026-03-10 - Integration iteration: Batch scheduler affinity implemented in canary. Observed 9% tail-latency improvement (p95) for canary customers and 22% reduction in repeated fragment transfers in controlled test. Moving to wider canary next sprint.
acceptance_criteria: LSH index produces stable cluster IDs for 99.9% of requests under normal traffic (same prefix variants map to same cluster)
Cluster manifest store scales to 10k clusters/shard with <10ms lookup latency
GPU prewarm profile reduces first-request slab transfer rate by >=20% in replayed production traces
Batch scheduler affinity increases intra-batch KV re-use rate by >=15% without regressing average latency SLO
All changes pass regression tests and have dashboards for cluster heat, prewarm success, and duplication ratio
